transcript:
Header: 2026-12-31 15:00 UTC | Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Liam Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Jordan Park (Redwood SE - first 10m), Alex Morales (Aurelia CTO), Rina Patel (ML Eng), Marcus Lee (Infra Lead), Sara Kim (Security), Diego (PM)

Summary: quick deck walkthrough then live demo with synthetic workload for long context + high TPS streaming. Questions on backpressure, timeouts, and how Redwood falls back across model variants.

[00:00] Liam Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, happy new year eve... I mean new year eve demo, hope everyone's good. quick agenda, priya will go through the runtime and then we'll do a live demo with our long context test and a simulated high-tps load.

[00:15] Priya Nair: Hi all, yeah I'll start with the architecture, sorry if audio is a bit low on my end. So Redwood's serving runtime handles large kv cache windows, we support persistent prefix caching, and we do automatic continuity batching. I'll call out some important behaviors under long context — for example the kernel selection changes as sequence length grows, and we prefer chunked attention for >64k tokens workloads.

[01:02] Alex Morales: Quick clarifying q, when you say chunked attention, does that mean we can do a single 100k token context read for a conversation? what's the throughput impact?

[01:18] Priya Nair: yes you can, it's supported as long as the model variant is compiled for long context, and we recommend a quantized variant for best memory profile. throughput will drop per-instance of course — you'll see longer per-request latency, but throughput per GPU can be kept sensible with continuous batching and prefix/KV caching. In our internal long-context perf sheet we showed X tokens/s for a 100k run on an A100V4. I'll send the exact numbers after.

[02:05] Rina Patel: Is the KV cache the same as the prefix cache — we have some stateful chat threads we want to keep resident for low-latency resumes.

[02:20] Priya Nair: yes — prefix cache, kv cache, we sometimes call it KV cash in quick notes (laughs) but same thing — it's resident across calls if you opt for session pinning on Dedicated. It reduces token generation cost for repeated contexts.

[03:10] Marcus Lee: gap in our infra question — for on-prem we are running a mix of RTX6000 and older A40s, plus some H100s in cloud. what's the compatibility story and recommended drivers?

[03:30] Priya Nair: good q — we have a compatibility checklist. briefly, for A40/RTX stacks we recommend CUDA 12.x and matching driver, container runtime runc or nvidia-container-runtime 1.5+, and for H100s we recommend the latest NCCL + interconnect tuning. We'll share the checklist. Some tuning for throughput (NVIDIA MIG vs full GPU) matters.

[04:05] Diego (PM): and KMS — if we want to keep keys on-prem, are you able to integrate with our HSM?

[04:12] Liam Chen: yes we support external KMS/HSM integrations via our private deployment. We can bind to your key provider and use envelope encryption. We'll include SSO and audit log notes in the security doc.

[05:00] Priya Nair: ok moving to demo. I'll spin a workload that simulates 1) a single long-context request (approx 80-120k tokens) and 2) a sustained high-tps stream at 800-1500 RPS with streaming responses enabled. Note: streaming here sends chunked tokens over a websocket; client side needs to handle backpressure and re-requests.

[05:45] [screen share begins — latency graphs and terminal logs visible]

[06:10] Priya Nair: starting long context run now — sending a synthetic doc and instructing model to run a summarization over the whole. You'll see memory climb as KV cache populates.

[06:30] Rina Patel: seeing some noisy logs in terminal… looks like you hit a GC?

[06:38] Priya Nair: yeah that's the runtime flushing intermediate buffers, we have dynamic memory compaction to avoid fragmentation; sometimes logs look scary but it's expected.

[07:05] [00:07:05] Jordan Park: I want to point out we have a fallback policy — if the long-context compiled model fails or hits OOM, the router can fallback to a compatible model with chunked summarization where we stream context windows and reassemble results. That reduces fidelity slightly but keeps the call alive.

[07:40] Alex Morales: how does that manifest to the client? is it a silent fallback or do we get an error that suggests retry?

[07:51] Priya Nair: we emit a status in the response metadata — if in streaming mode we send a final control frame indicating fallback and reason. Clients can register on the stream to receive that. We can also do automatic chunking at the gateway if you prefer no client changes.

[08:30] [first long-context response completes — partial tokens streaming into the terminal]

[09:00] Rina Patel: quality looks ok, there are a few hallucinated dates in the summarization — is there a way to tune generation constraints for long contexts?

[09:12] Priya Nair: yes we expose generation params (temperature, repetition penalty, logit bias) and also provide an idea of what prompt truncation or windowing we used. In long-context mode we often bias older tokens lower to avoid stale facts being over-weighted.

[10:00] Liam Chen: switching to the high-tps test — we'll enable streaming and start an 800 RPS load from our benchmarker which simulates many short chat requests with 512 token context each, plus some pinned sessions to exercise cached kvs.

[10:20] [load generator started — graphs spike to 800 RPS, then ramp to 1.4k RPS]

[11:00] Marcus Lee: at 1.4k we see some increasing latencies around p99 — is that expected?

[11:10] Priya Nair: yes, p99 increases with queueing; we have few levers: increase pooling / reserved capacity, tune batch windows, or accept slight p99 tail. Redwood also supports request routing by latency tier — you can send critical low-latency requests to a low-batch lane.

[11:45] Alex Morales: about streaming backpressure — what happens when the client is slow to consume? do you queue up tokens or drop?

[12:00] Priya Nair: good question. By default we buffer a small window on the server side then apply backpressure to the model engine if the client is not ACKing fast enough. For websocket streaming we also support a windowed flow control: client advertises buffer capacity and server respects it. If the client is too slow we can escalate by dropping non-critical intermediate frames and eventually cut to a non-streaming single final response or return an explicit timeout error.

[12:45] Sara Kim: does that behavior cause lost audit logs or inconsistent billing? we need auditability for compliance.

[12:55] Liam Chen: no — every request and final outcome is logged. If a stream is cut due to client backpressure, the event, reason, and partial token counts are recorded in the audit logs. Billing is correlated to final token counts and we provide a reconciliation report for pilots.

[13:40] Rina Patel: is there an SDK that handles the windowed flow control for websockets? we don't want to implement that ourselves if it's tricky.

[13:52] Priya Nair: yes our JS and Python SDKs include streaming helpers that implement the flow control handshake and auto-retry semantics for transient timeouts. They also surface events like fallback and partial results. We'll share the SDK snippet.

[14:30] [load spikes, a few connections show WARN: streaming backpressure exceeded threshold]

[14:50] Priya Nair: ok we intentionally let one connection hit the threshold to show behavior — see stream id 0x1f... it transitioned to compressed final response and emitted a 408 timeout. note that the client could choose to re-request the remainder using the session pin id.

[15:30] Marcus Lee: would that partial 408 cause us to lose the slot and penalize throughput? if our clients are flaky we could see a lot of slot thrashing.

[15:45] Priya Nair: we thought of that — we have short circuit policies: if we detect repeated client-side slow consumers we can move them to a low-priority queue, or shard sessions so flaky clients don't hold hot GPU slots. It's configurable per-customer.

[16:20] Alex Morales: curious about cost — if we do a pilot with 1.4k RPS sustained for a week, what's the cost ballpark compared to a hosted API?

[16:35] Liam Chen: for Dedicated or Private the unit economics differ; hosted is pay-as-you-go but higher per-token; Dedicated has commit pricing — I'll send the pilot pricing sheet with modeled throughput numbers. We'll show an example where Dedicated with 8xA100V4 yields better cost per million tokens at sustained high throughput.

[17:05] Rina Patel: another question: when you degrade to a smaller model, do you preserve the streaming interface? we need to keep UX consistent.

[17:20] Priya Nair: yes we maintain the same streaming contract; only the model quality and latency change. There's also an option to return an early metadata field telling clients that the model quality tier changed.

[18:00] [demo continues — team toggles autoscaling and shows burst capacity kicking in]

[18:30] Priya Nair: here you see autoscale policy — we can provision reserved slots for steady traffic and a burst pool for short spikes; burst pool uses a lower-cost preemptible capacity usually.

[19:10] Marcus Lee: any network limits we need to open? our infra team has restrictive egress rules.

[19:20] Liam Chen: for Private you can run everything inside your VPC, so no egress required. For Dedicated we have peering options; we'll include the specific ports and peering notes in the compatibility doc.

[20:05] Sara Kim: SOC2 and log retention — do you retain raw transcript? we can't have customer PII logged unencrypted.

[20:20] Liam Chen: default retention is configurable; for Private deployments you control retention. For hosted we offer encryption at rest and we can redact or not store transcripts based on your policy. We'll share the compliance pack.

[21:00] [noise in connection, brief dropout between 21:00 and 21:18]

[21:25] Diego: quick ask — can you demonstrate a simulated client that times out mid-stream and then resumes using the session id?

[21:40] Priya Nair: yeah pulling up session pin demo — see client disconnect, then we reattach to the session id and request missing tokens; runtime will serve from pinned kv if available and resume.

[22:30] Rina Patel: ok that addresses a lot. for our production UX we prefer the client not to worry about partials; does Redwood provide a library to rehydrate final assembled responses server-side?

[22:45] Priya Nair: we have a server-side helper that can consume partial streams and reassemble them into a canonical final response, with dedupe heuristics for overlapping chunks. We'll share code.

[23:30] Alex Morales: security question — do you support SAML 2.0 SSO for console and RBAC for model access?

[23:45] Liam Chen: yes, both. RBAC is configurable by route/model and we emit per-token audit traces.

[24:10] [Priya toggles latency vs cost graph; shows Optimize recommendations for batching / quantization profiles]

[24:40] Priya Nair: this is Redwood Optimize — given your workload profile (long contexts + many short chats) we recommend a hybrid model floor: long-context variant for heavy sessions + small quantized variant for the front-line short chats. Optimize will propose quantization and batching params to hit your p95/p99 targets while minimizing chip-hours.

[25:20] Rina Patel: curious if Optimize can run on our historical traces?

[25:28] Priya Nair: yes you can upload a sample of traces or point to a superset; Optimize will run simulated workloads and give a recommended config and cost estimate.

[26:00] [second load run — intentionally create client-side slowdown on 3% of connections to show backpressure policies]

[26:30] [logs show flow control handshake and a few 408s; one stream shows 'partial-compressed-response' code]

[27:10] Marcus Lee: I see logs flagged 'client-backpressure' — can we route those to a debug-only logging sink? we don't want normal ops to be noisy.

[27:25] Priya Nair: yes, you can route different log levels to separate sinks and apply sampling. We also provide per-route error budgets and alerting hooks into your pager.

[28:00] Alex Morales: let's talk timeline — if a pilot looks good, what's a reasonable timeline to go from pilot to production for Private?

[28:15] Liam Chen: for Private deployments it typically takes 4-8 weeks after pilot depending on approvals and infra procurement; Dedicated is usually faster if you take reserved capacity. We'll layout the milestone plan in the pricing doc.

[29:00] Sara Kim: last compliance Q — do you support customer-managed key rotation schedules?

[29:12] Liam Chen: yes, rotation is supported; for Private you can rotate and we integrate with common HSMs. We'll include rotation examples in the security pack.

[30:00] [demo wrap-up — Priya shows final perf numbers and savings from batch tuning]

[30:40] Priya Nair: final notes — under sustained 1.4k RPS with batching tuned, our p50/p95 looks good and cost per token reduces ~30% compared to naive per-request mode. For long contexts we recommend mixing quantized LLMs and chunked summarization for best tradeoffs.

[31:10] Alex Morales: ok what's next — we want pricing and the exact compatibility checklist, plus to lock a window for the pilot Jan 10-17.

[31:30] Liam Chen: noted. we'll send the pricing/perf spreadsheet and compatibility checklist. Marcus, can you confirm your infra windows by early Jan?

[31:40] Marcus Lee: yes I'll take that offline and confirm by Jan 4.

[32:00] Diego: will you also include a sample of the streaming SDK code? our frontend team needs to integrate.

[32:10] Priya Nair: yes JS and Python SDK snippets included.

[32:40] [short recap by Liam]

[33:00] Liam Chen: recap: 1) we'll send pricing & perf sheet; 2) Priya will share compatibility checklist and SDK snippets; 3) Marcus to confirm pilot dates; 4) Sara to share compliance matrix. Pilot kickoff tentatively Jan 10. I'll follow up in email with attachments and a calendar invite.

[33:35] Alex Morales: thanks all — good session, fair few details we need but overall looks promising.

[33:50] Rina Patel: quick one — can you include an example of a chunked summarization prompt so we can test local?

[34:05] Priya Nair: yes will include prompt templates and an eval harness for regression checks.

[34:30] [call winds down, small casual chatter, signoffs]

[57:00] End: recording stopped

Notes: transcription has minor mis-hearings (e.g., 'KV cash'), some overlapped speech, and occasional truncated timestamps. Shared artifacts referenced: Redwood long-context perf spreadsheet (link: https://redwood.example/perf/aurelia-long-context), compatibility checklist doc (link: https://redwood.example/docs/aurelia-compat), Redwood security pack (link: https://redwood.example/security-pack).
questions: How does Redwood handle streaming backpressure without losing audit logs?
What are the recommended drivers and runtimes for mixed A40/H100 on-prem clusters?
How are fallbacks surfaced to clients during long-context OOMs?
